Data Interpretation Activity: Wave-Particle Duality of Light

Introduction

This activity introduces students to the wave-particle duality of light by examining mock data tables and graphs comparing the frequency and amplitude of light waves and their abilities to (a) damage living cells and (b) activate the photoelectric effect.

Table 1: Effects of Light on Living Cells

Light Source Frequency (Hz) Amplitude Exposure Time (seconds) Cell Damage Observed (Yes/No) Damage Level (Scale: Low, Medium, High)
Red Laser 14.3 x 10^{14} 560 No    
Red Laser 24.3 x 10^{14} 1560 No    
Green Laser 15.5 x 10^14 560 No    
Green Laser 25.5 x 10^14 1560 No

Graph IdeasYou can have students create the following types of graphs:For Cell Damage:Bar Graph 1: Frequency on the x-axis, Cell Damage Level on the y-axis (grouping by similar frequencies). This should show a trend of higher frequency leading to more damage.Scatter Plot 1: Amplitude on the x-axis, Cell Damage Level on the y-axis (grouping by similar frequencies). This should show that while higher amplitude might increase the extent of damage at damaging frequencies, it doesn’t cause damage at lower frequencies.For Photoelectric Effect:Scatter Plot 2: Frequency on the x-axis, Kinetic Energy of Ejected Electrons on the y-axis. This should show a positive correlation, with a threshold frequency below which no electrons are ejected. Amplitude should not affect the kinetic energy.Bar Graph 2: Frequency on the x-axis, Number of Ejected Electrons on the y-axis (comparing different amplitudes at the same frequency above the threshold). This should show that at frequencies above the threshold, higher amplitude leads to more ejected electrons.Bar Graph 3: Amplitude on the x-axis, Number of Ejected Electrons on the y-axis (grouping by similar frequencies above the threshold). This should clearly demonstrate the direct relationship between amplitude and the number of ejected electrons (intensity).Analysis Questions for StudentsRelating to Cell Damage:Observe Table 1 and Graph 1. What general trend do you notice between the frequency of light and the likelihood and level of cell damage?Examine the data for the red and green lasers (different amplitudes, similar lower frequencies). Does increasing the amplitude of these lower-frequency lights cause cell damage in this experiment? What does this suggest about the primary factor determining whether light can damage cells in this scenario?Compare the UV lamp data points with different amplitudes. Does a higher amplitude UV light cause more severe damage? How does this relate to your answer in question 2?Based on this data, is the energy carried by a light wave solely determined by its amplitude? Explain your reasoning. Consider how different frequencies behave.How might the frequency of light be related to the energy of individual “packets” of light (photons) interacting with the cells?Relating to the Photoelectric Effect:Observe Table 2 and Graph 2. What is the relationship between the frequency of light and the kinetic energy of the ejected electrons? What happens below a certain frequency?Compare the data for the red light with the green, blue, and UV light. Even with a higher amplitude, red light does not eject electrons. What does this imply about the role of frequency in initiating the photoelectric effect?Examine the data for the green, blue, and UV light sources at different amplitudes (Graph 3). What effect does increasing the amplitude have on the number of ejected electrons? What does this suggest about the intensity of the light?Does changing the amplitude of the light change the kinetic energy of the individual ejected electrons? Support your answer with evidence from Table 2 and Graph 2.

Based on these data, what two properties of light seem to be important in the photoelectric effect? What does this suggest about the nature of light interacting with electrons?How does the photoelectric effect data suggest that light might behave as particles (photons) rather than just waves? Consider how the energy transfer seems to be quantized (specific amounts related to frequency).Bridging the Two Phenomena:In both the cell damage and photoelectric effect experiments, does the amplitude of light always have the same effect? Explain.How does the concept of a “threshold” (seen in the photoelectric effect) relate to the idea that only certain frequencies of light can cause cell damage?Based on your analysis of both datasets, can you propose a model where light exhibits both wave-like and particle-like properties? How might frequency and amplitude relate to the energy and number of these “particles”?
